newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks' reputation seen at low over Holocaust.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks' reputation seen at low over Holocaust.

text.p: Swiss banks have lost so much credibility over their handling of Holocaust accounts that only an international investigation now under way can restore it, bankers and Jewish leaders said on Thursday.

One day after Swiss banks lifted their traditional secrecy to publish names of lost account holders, critics said the revelations had proven the necessity of an international commission led by former U.S. central bank head Paul Volcker.

A widescale audit of Swiss vaults has been started by Volcker's mixed commission of Swiss and international Jewish representatives, created last year under pressure led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC).

The Swiss Bankers Association, which groups the country's 400 financial institutes, acknowledged that it was now up to these outside experts to tell the world whether the banks had come clean or whether they were hiding more dormant wealth.
"Our efforts continue and we do not work alone but rather together with the auditors and the Volcker commission," association chairman Georg Krayer told Swiss television.
"I believe it is up to them in the end to establish whether our credibility is sufficient or not," he said.
The unprecedented publication of the accounts list of over 1,870 names has backfired in two ways, critics said.
It proved the banks had had enough information over the years to try and contact clients or heirs if they had not heard from the owners after World War Two.

It also forced the banks to acknowledge the total of dormant pre-1945 accounts opened by foreigners was 61.2 million Swiss francs, nearly 20 million or 40 percent more than they had reported last year,
"The credibility of the banks is shattered," Thomas Lyssy, vice-president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG), told Reuters.
"I think there is trust in the Volcker commission on the part of Jewish groups....We need supervision of the banks and an active search for dormant accounts," he said,

In Paris, secretary-general Serge Cwajenbaum of the European Jewish Congress said the banks' new openness had to be weighed against the fact that Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) was caught in January shredding World War Two-era documents.
"All the truth has not yet come out. To get to the truth, whatever it is, we need total transparency and so far, we have seen few signs of this," he told the newspaper France-Soir.
Germany's daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung commented, "The Swiss had to be dragged and beaten before they moved, tiny step by tiny step, to the names of those murdered and deprived of their rights."

The global publication of the bank list, covering accounts opened by foreigners before World War Two ended in Europe in May 1945, was the start of an effort to return lost wealth that grew out of the Volcker commission's work.

International interest in the list, which will be followed in October by a second one of dormant accounts opened by Swiss residents, showed in over 2,000 phone calls in the first day and half to five global contact centres in New York, Basle, Budapest, Tel Aviv and Sydney.
The Swiss Bankers Association also said the Internet site for the list at www.dormantaccounts.ch saw one million "hits", or requests for information, in its first 36 hours.
Volcker's commission of seven members, including three named by world Jewish groups and three by Swiss banks, was created last year.

It is now directing teams of international auditors doing test audits at sample Swiss banks to determine the extent of full-scale inquiries due to start thi year, with an eye to completing the work in mid-1998.
